author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: Emma Woodhouse, handsome, clever, and rich, with a comfortable home and happy disposition, seemed to unite some of the best blessings of existence; and had lived nearly twenty-one years in the world with very little to distress or vex her. She was the absolute mistress of her domain, directing the affairs of her father's household with a confidence that rarely admitted the possibility of error.

author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: She was the youngest of the two daughters of a most affectionate, indulgent father; and had, in consequence of her sister's marriage, been mistress of his house from a very early period. Her mother had died too long ago for her to have more than an indistinct remembrance of her caresses; and her place had been supplied by an excellent woman as governess, who had fallen little short of a mother in affection.

author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: Sixteen years had Miss Taylor been in Mr. Woodhouse's family, less as a governess than a friend, very fond of both daughters, but particularly of Emma. Between them it was more the intimacy of sisters. Even before Miss Taylor had ceased to hold the nominal office of governess, the mildness of her temper had hardly allowed her to impose any restraint; and the shadow of authority being now long passed away, they had been living together as friend and friend very mutually attached, and Emma doing just what she liked.

author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: The real evils, indeed, of Emma's situation were the power of having rather too much her own way, and a disposition to think a little too well of herself; these were the disadvantages which threatened alloy to her many enjoyments. The danger, however, was at present so unperceived, that they did not by any means rank as misfortunes with her.

author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: Sorrow came—a gentle sorrow—but not at all in the shape of any disagreeable consciousness.—Miss Taylor married. It was Miss Taylor's loss which first brought grief. It was on the wedding-day of this beloved friend that Emma first sat in mournful thought of any continuance. The wedding over, and the bride-people gone, her father and herself were left to dine together, with no prospect of a third to cheer a long evening.

author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: The event had every promise of happiness for her friend. Mr. Weston was a man of unexceptionable character, easy fortune, suitable age, and pleasant manners; and there was some satisfaction in considering with what self-denying, generous friendship she had always wished and promoted the match; but it was a black morning's work for her. The want of Miss Taylor would be felt every hour of every day.

author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: How she was to bear the change was a question of some anxiety; for though Mrs. Weston was but half a mile distant, Emma was acutely aware of the difference between a friend in the neighborhood and a friend in the house, especially as her father's conversational powers were notably deficient, rendering him an entirely unequal companion.

author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: Mr. Woodhouse's habits as a valetudinarian, lacking both mental and physical vigor, effectively doubled the disparity of their ages; and while his amiable temper secured universal affection, his talents could never have recommended him at any time as an engaging or stimulating companion for a young woman of Emma's intellect.

author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: Her sister, being established in London some sixteen miles distant, was removed far beyond the convenience of daily intercourse; leaving Emma to anticipate many a long, unbroken, and solitary autumn evening before the Christmas holidays might afford her the relief of society and the bustling arrival of Isabella's family.

author: Jane Austen
ai_styled_text: Highbury afforded no equals, and certainly no substitute for Miss Taylor. It was a melancholy prospect, yet Emma was obliged to stifle her sighs and assume a cheerful countenance; for Mr. Woodhouse, whose gentle selfishness made him a bitter enemy to change of any kind, could not speak of the marriage without profound compassion for the bride's supposed misfortune, and Emma knew she must exert herself to dispel his gloom.
